reader_notes: Technically sound in a way that survives checking: the five partials named (hum, prime, minor third, fifth, nominal an octave above the prime) are the standard true-harmonic stack, tuning by removing metal from the inner wall is how it is really done, and 'nothing pulls it back up' is the correct one-way constraint. Nothing here reads as invented.

The economics are stated crisply and then used - bronze billed by the kilo, tuning by the hour, and lathe time not scaling with weight. q1 tests exactly that asymmetry, and C is the intuitive-but-wrong scaling assumption a reader will bring in from outside.

q3 is a properly inferential item. The text never says 'a founder who tunes all five tightly must cast heavier'; the reader has to join the casting allowance, the one-way arrow, and the 'four kilos apart at the pour' in the final paragraph. Satisfying to solve and hard to guess.
Arithmetic reconciles: 240 kg off the mould, 228 kg finished, 12 kg of allowance.

q4 is fair because the writer's restraint is genuinely on the page - Voregg is given the line that limits the Ockthorne trial ('One afternoon, one tower, bells of different weights'), and the writer separately notes that the decisive two-bell experiment has never been paid for. B is ruled out precisely by that sentence: the question is not called unsettleable, only unfunded.
'You can hear a bell that has been argued with' is a strong line and does not feel machine-made.
The closing image (the bin of turnings about a third full) ties back to the recovered-scrap paragraph without being asked to carry a question. Good texture discipline.
